newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Bulgarians scramble for funds in chaotic economy.
newsitem.headline: Bulgarians scramble for funds in chaotic economy.

text.p: Bulgarians queued on Thursday for treasury bonds yielding 450 percent per annum, some cashed levs for dollars and self-described "criminals" blamed the government for the country's state of near fiscal chaos.

"It's very bad," accountant Valentin Grigorov said as he stood in a line of about 150 people at the Bulgarian National Bank (BNB) building in Sofia to buy treasury paper which, he said, with compounded interest could yield 450 percent annum.
Elsewhere around town, people could be seen exchanging their levs for dollars at 24-hour change shops.

The BNB, grappling with bank insolvency and the collapse of the lev which plummeted from 70 to the dollar in January to about 230 this week, on Monday effectively closed nine banks by putting them under state supervision and hiked the central bank interest rate to an all-time high of 300 percent.

The measures were designed to convince the International Monetary Fund (IMF), meeting in Washington next week, to release a second $115 million tranche of a standby loan. The IMF postponed the tranche until Bulgaria closed 64 loss-making state enterprises and stabilised its financial system.
Western diplomats said they thought the measures would convince the IMF to release the funds.
"That's why they are doing all these drastic steps and it seems reasonable to think they should get it," a diplomat said.
But the expense in human terms is soaring in Sofia where people are unable to make ends meet on average monthly salaries of 12,000 levs, now worth just over $50.
"One kilo (2.2 pounds) of meat costs 800 levs and people don't have enough money to pay for heat and electricity," said the owner of a small restaurant who gave his name as Stefan.
"Many Bulgarian people are going crazy because there's just no money."
But the restaurateur and others think there is money to spare, only it is being siphoned out of the mainstream economy.

"We are the criminals," Ivo Karamanski, head of an insurance company called Crown Ins, said in an ironic tone as he had dinner with a half dozen people in the wine bar of Sofia's elegant Sheraton hotel.

Karamanski said he was a well-known figure around Sofia, with much speculation in the Bulgarian press about the source of his wealth, but he said Bulgaria's current state "is the fault of the government".
"The money goes abroad because the big communists go abroad," he said, pointing the finger at the ruling socialist party, composed largely of former communists.

"This country doesn't export anything and all the prices of everything go up," added his associate, Kingsley Boaima, a Liberian who said he was once associated with the rebel faction there headed by Charles Taylor.

Diplomats said the government was at least partially to blame for the current state of affairs, but that measures including restructuring the banking system, selling off state enterprises and hiking the value added tax as well as petrol prices and electric rates, should do the trick.
"The socialists came relatively late to these reforms and only did it under the pressure of running out of money," a diplomat said.
"But it's a very heavy load for an economy in poor shape to begin with and for a population that has seen that the changes after communism have not benefited the people."
